body: On the whiteboard in the church hall, left over from a leaders’ meeting that overran, is a diagram somebody drew while explaining something: five boxes, one under the other, joined by a vertical line, a word written in each. It is a quarter past nine. Four of them are still by the door talking about a car, and the urn has been switched off and is making the noise urns make. A man stacking chairs photographs the board first, because a woman who had to leave early asked him to. Then he finds the cloth and wipes it, and stacks the last of the chairs, and turns the lights off on his way out.

Nobody in that room set out to invent a chain of command. It happened on a whiteboard in about forty seconds, and it happened because the boxes were drawn one above another rather than side by side. Nearly every misreading of the five-fold begins at exactly that moment, with a marker pen and no malice whatsoever.

Apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers. The list is short, it appears once, and it comes with its purpose attached in the same sentence: these are given for the equipping of the saints for the work of ministry.

The word worth taking literally is fold. A fivefold cord, a fivefold blessing, a cloth folded five times — a fold is a pleat, not a storey. Fivefold means having five parts, all of them the same cloth, none of them on top of any other. The English has drifted because we now hear anything numbered as something ranked, and because titles are the easiest part of a list to keep. But look at what the purpose clause does. If all five exist to equip the saints for the work, then all five are service functions and the congregation is doing the ministry. A structure in which the named people are the servants is not a hierarchy drawn upside down. It is not a hierarchy.

This band takes that seriously enough to have been built on it. The band runs from HM 300 to HM 400 and is divided into five blocks of twenty whole numbers, one block per office. The Crossing, HM 300 to HM 320, is the evangelist. The Nations, HM 320 to HM 340, is the apostle. The Upper Room, HM 340 to HM 360, is the prophet. The Living Room, HM 360 to HM 380, is the shepherd. The Table, HM 380 to HM 400, is the teacher.

Notice the widths. Each block is twenty units, and not one of them is wider than the others. There is no premium stretch of dial for the apostolic block and no cramped corner for the pastoral one. That was a decision and an expensive one, because the blocks are not equally full and never will be; a scheme that allocated space by demand would have carved this up quite differently and looked more efficient doing it. The passage names five things the church needs done. It does not name five ranks, and it does not put anybody above anybody — and a band that gave one office more room than another would be arguing the opposite every time somebody looked at it.

The ranked reading is not the only misuse and may not be the worst one. The subtler failure is to treat the five as personality types — sit the assessment, discover you are a prophet, and organise your self-image around the result. That turns a description of work the church needs into a description of what a person is, and the two are not the same thing at all. Function is assigned to a body by need. Identity is not. A congregation that has worked out what everybody is has usually stopped asking what is missing, which was the only question the list was any use for.

There is a further detail in how the band is laid out that gives the game away. The five blocks are not in the order the passage lists them. They ascend by listener journey instead: music at the low end that draws somebody in, then the languages of the world, then prayer, then family and care, then teaching and substance at the top. Read from the bottom up, the dial traces a discipleship path rather than an org chart. And that reordering is the point — it was done for a listener’s convenience, and nothing broke.
That is worth sitting with. You cannot reorder a hierarchy. Try it and the thing stops working, because the order was the content.

The ranked reading is trying to answer a real question and deserves better than mockery. Churches do need to know who decides, who is accountable to whom, and what happens when a leader goes wrong. Scripture is not silent about oversight; there are elders, there is appointing, there is correction, and a community with no answer to any of that is not humble but negligent. So the instinct behind the pyramid is sound. The trouble is that it borrows a passage answering a completely different question. Ask the five-fold who is in charge and it will not tell you, because it was never a list of ranks. It was a list of the work.
The passage names five things the church needs done. It does not name five ranks.

A woman who is seventy-one has run the Sunday children’s hour for longer than the current minister has been ordained. She arrives at twenty past nine with a plastic crate whose lid does not match, containing a tambourine missing one jingle, a felt board repaired with parcel tape, and a biscuit tin of crayons in which there are eleven blues and no red. She knows which child cannot have nuts, which one will not sit down, and which one has been quiet for three weeks and why. In two decades she has been asked to say something from the front perhaps four times. Nobody has ever asked her what her office is, and if they did she would say she helps out with the children.

That is the shepherd function, running at full capacity, entirely unlabelled. On this band it is not a footnote under something more important. It is a block twenty units wide with its own colour, and the whole of The Living Room sits in it.

Here is the honest part, and it is uncomfortable because it is checkable. One of the five blocks on this dial is still silent. HM 383.20 Jubilee Teaching, up in The Table, is assigned and nothing is playing on it today. The prophetic block stood the same way until this year, when HM 350.00 The Upper Room — the prayer station the block is named after — went on air carrying sung Scripture prayer; that leaves the teaching office as the one still allocated and unsounded. Four offices are sounding. One is not.

That is not a fault in the structure. It is the structure doing its one job. A list of five functions is useful precisely because it lets a community notice which ones are absent, and a dial that shows the gap as a quiet stretch of band is doing what the passage was for. Most churches are short of at least two of the five, and noticing which two is considerably more productive than working out which one you are. A church can tell itself a story about its gaps for twenty years. A band cannot. Silence on a frequency is very hard to argue with.

So the five-fold is not an org chart, and the strongest evidence for that is not an argument at all — it is a picture. Lay the five out in a column and you get a career ladder that has produced a century of title inflation. Lay them out side by side, in equal widths, across a band that anybody can turn, and the whole misreading becomes impossible to hold. You cannot climb sideways. You can only tune.
All of which stays theoretical until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

46 of the band’s 121 frequencies are on air. The Nations is the fullest by a clear margin, running language by language across its twenty units. The Crossing comes next, because music in the language of the place is where a band starts — praise and worship, gospel country, Christian rap, Afro-Caribbean, Messianic. The Living Room is the smallest of the sounding three and the easiest to underestimate, which is precisely the point of what follows.

Start at HM 361.90, Jubilee Kids Party. It sits in The Living Room, which is the shepherd’s block, and it is the last place a person hunting for a hierarchy would think to look — which is the reason to go there first. Put it on with children in the room and hear what it actually is: not a lesser version of the grown-up stations, not a holding pen until real ministry starts, but the pastoral function at full strength and full volume. It is a party and it is unembarrassed about being one. If the five are five ranks, this frequency is near the bottom of them and you can safely skip it. If the five are five kinds of work a church cannot do without, this is one of them, sounding across exactly the same width of band as the apostolic block further down the dial.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download, no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive devices and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add it to your home screen if you want it closer to hand. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are reaching for — which is how the two silent blocks get filled in.

So treat this as an invitation rather than an argument won. Do not go and work out which of the five you are; that is the assessment-quiz reading and it has never once helped anybody. Put HM 361.90 on this Saturday morning, and then turn the dial slowly from one end of the band to the other and count what you can hear and what you cannot. Twenty units, five times over, no box above any other box. Whatever you find missing on the dial, you will probably find missing somewhere nearer to hand as well.
